description: Hi! I'm Pritidipa, a high school student from Bangladesh with interdisciplinary interests in astrophysics, chemistry...I'm particularly fascinated by how we can use computational methods to uncover things that are otherwise difficult to observe.I like creating different ways of making complex scientific information more accessible.For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, I'm excited about creating an interactive, scientifically grounded project. I'm looking forward to meeting people.
summary: You can’t blink SPHEREx: a different filter colour sits over every pixel, so two exposures of one star can differ when nothing in the sky changed. Nakshatra CHRONOS is an open web observatory that finds real change anyway. It compares only fair pairs (same array, matched colour, compatible release) with three independent methods, and treats their disagreement as evidence. On simulated fields with a hidden answer key, changes flagged by all three were real 91% of the time; anomaly only flags, 5%. Each candidate gets a 102 channel spectral history, ten instrument forensics tests, six separate confidence scores, a ranked next observation and an evidence passport verifiable with sha256sum. CHRONOS also tests itself on real data. It checks each SPHEREx exposure against NASA’s calibration files and measures how far each calibration step can shift a result. The archive’s noise estimate runs 2–25% low, so a 5σ detection may really be closer to 4σ. Across one real frame, it found half of planted sources at about 0.2 mJy. Before calling anything a mover, it shuffles the observation dates; if the movers survive shuffled dates, they were coincidences, and it says so. Earlier, it found 29 of 120 planted sources and answered - unknown rather than guess. That discipline matters for faint, slow targets like Planet X, and for students and citizen scientists who want to check a claim, not take it on trust.
details:
What it does

SPHEREx maps the entire sky in 102 colours, covering wavelengths from 0.75 to 5 microns. Each of its six detectors has a filter, allowing different detector positions to measure different wavelengths. When the telescope observes the same star again, the star will usually fall on a different part of the filter. As a result, it may be measured at a different wavelength. This can make the star appear to change in brightness even when the source itself has not changed. Such false variability can appear frequently when two SPHEREx images are directly compared. CHRONOS is designed to account for these effects and distinguish genuine changes from apparent ones.

How it works

CHRONOS reads all available exposures for a region of the sky, along with their associated data layers: image, flags, variance, zodiacal light, PSF and wavelength map. It checks whether the estimated noise in each exposure agrees with its actual scatter. It also assesses how reliably the observations can be associated with Gaia stars.

Only compatible observations are compared. They must come from the same array, the same colour and the same data release.

Three independent methods then search for changes:

  1. A PSF based catalogue method with a motion consistency assessment.
  2. The Honest Noise Model (HNM) based difference image method.
  3. An anomaly detection ensemble.

Each method has different failure modes. Their agreements and disagreements are therefore treated as evidence rather than ignored. In simulations with hidden ground truth labels, all three methods flagged 91% of the changes, while 5% were flagged only by the anomaly ensemble.

A classification engine evaluates five possible explanations: moving, variable, transient, artefact and nothing. It can also return "unknown" when the available evidence is insufficient.

CHRONOS also checks its own classifications. It performs tests that were not used during the initial classification, repeats the analysis using 11 other reasonable configurations and compares the assessments of the motion, photometry and instrument analysis modules.

The BDI brings together CHRONOS 4D and ten analytical laboratories. Each candidate is examined across four dimensions: space, time, wavelength and evidence.

Spectral history

This laboratory presents a 102 channel record of flux and uncertainty over time. It includes a heatmap, time slider, difference view and stability score. These features help determine whether apparent variability comes from wavelength sampling or calibration effects. The empty channels 51 and 52 in DR1 remain visibly empty. They are never filled with estimated values.

Instrument forensics

Ten diagnostic tests examine crosstalk, aurora, helium at 1.083 microns, shuttle glow, dead pixels, nonlinearity, read noise, gain, zodiacal light and PSF.

Each test is linked to an official SPHEREx calibration file that can be used to verify the relevant effect. In the practice field, these checks reduce the number of raw detections from 319 to four sky candidates.

Next observation

This laboratory compares possible follow up observations according to the information they could provide.

Ice band depth laboratory

Examines water, CO₂, CO and methanol absorption bands.

Planet X laboratory

Reexamines the IRAS and AKARI candidate pair, separated by 47.46 arcminutes and based on observations taken 23 years apart. It also explains why two observed positions alone cannot determine an orbit.

Case studies

Includes selected cases involving 3I/ATLAS, young stars, brown dwarfs and Miras.

Evidence passport

Every candidate receives a sealed evidence record. Each section is hashed using SHA256, allowing its integrity to be checked in a browser or with sha256sum.

Real NASA data

SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 are the default live search sources. CHRONOS has also been tested against data retrieved from NASA archives. These include:

  • 226 DR1 and 110 QR3 images of RW Aurigae.
  • A real DR1 All Sky Cube spectrum.
  • 12 nearby SPLICES ice targets.
  • Official calibration files for DR1 helium, aurora, shuttle glow, dead pixels, wavelength, ePSF and crosstalk.

The following animation shows selected SPHEREx DR1 images obtained at the JPL Horizons positions of 3I/ATLAS in August 2025.

New in the final version: testing on real exposures

Real frames

Three sky fields were tested: NEP, M101 and SEP. Each includes six full native SPHEREx frames with recorded file checksums. The NEP field contains three observations spanning 11 months.

The archive noise estimates were found to be approximately 2% to 25% lower than the observed noise. This means that a nominal 5σ detection could have an actual significance as low as approximately 4σ.

The zodiacal light model is the only component left out of the subtraction. This leaves a faint residual sky background. CHRONOS now addresses this with a source masked local background estimate.

Real completeness curve

In one real SEP frame, sources were planted across four zones to measure the recovery rate. Approximately 50% were recovered at 0.2 mJy and 94% at 0.8 mJy.

Chance controls

Before identifying anything as a moving source, CHRONOS shuffles the observation dates to check whether apparent motion could occur by chance.

When the dates of the three NEP observations were shuffled, the same number of apparent slow movers appeared as in the original sequence. These detections are therefore treated as possible chance alignments rather than confirmed moving sources.

Earlier real data test

In an earlier experiment, 120 sources were planted in actual QR3 images. CHRONOS recovered 29. Rather than making a stronger claim than the results supported, it returned "unknown" instead of forcing a classification.

Impact

CHRONOS produces a shortlist of candidates, possible explanations, uncertainties and suggested follow up observations for astronomers.

It also gives students and amateur skywatchers access to an astronomical research laboratory in both English and Bangla. They can examine the evidence, explore the results and take part in interpreting what the data show.

If Planet X exists, it would initially appear in CHRONOS as a candidate requiring further investigation, not as a discovery. This is a candidate based reporting system, and the project makes no claim of having discovered the planet.

What makes it creative

We identify three distinctive ideas in this combination of methods for SPHEREx.

  1. The fair pair rule, which ensures that only compatible observations are compared.
  2. Treating disagreements among three independent detection methods as measurable evidence.
  3. A system that actively challenges its own results, including by shuffling observation times.
Tools

Python, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, astroquery, astropy healpix, scikit learn, photutils, FastAPI, plain JavaScript with canvas charts, pytest with 188 automated tests, GitHub Pages, GitHub Actions, Kaggle notebooks and Docker. No additional hardware is required.

What we considered

Real astronomical data are not the same as simulations, so we report results from both.

Data releases are not combined without first checking their compatibility.

An archive outage does not mean that the sky is empty. It means that data are missing.

Every measurement has an uncertainty. Every reported number comes from either an actual measurement or an explicitly stated assumption.
